# Riemann Integration

Let $f:[a,b]\to \mathbb{R}$ be a bounded (not necessarily continuous) function
on a compact (closed, bounded) interval. We will define what it means for $f$
to be **Riemann integrable** on $[a,b]$ and, in that case, define its Riemann
integral $\int_a^b f$. The integral of $f$ on $[a,b]$ is a real number whose
geometrical interpretation is the signed area under the graph $y=f(x)$ for
$a\leq x\leq b$.

The Riemann integral is the simplest integral to define and it allows one to
integrate every continuous function as well as some not-too-badly discontinuous
functions. For highly discontinuous functions however it is insufficient and we
instead turn to the [[lebesgue-integral]] which is more flexible with better
mathematical properties.

## Riemann Integral

We say that two intervals are almost disjoint if they are disjoint or intersect
only at a common endpoint.  

:::{.definition data-title="Partition"}

Let $I$ be a nonempty compact interval. A **partition** of $I$ is a finite
collection $\{I_1, ..., I_n\}$ of almost disjoint, nonempty, compact
subintervals whose union is $I$.

:::

We denote a partition of $[a,b]$ by with subintervals $I_k=[x_{k-1},x_k]$
either by the collection of intervals
$$
\mathcal{P}=\{I_1, ..., I_n\},
$$
or by the set of endpoints
$$
\mathcal{P}=\{a=x_0 < x_1 < \cdots< x_n = b\}.
$$
Note that the sum of lengths $|I_k|=x_k-x_{k-1}$ of the almost disjoint
subintervals in a partition of an interval is equal to the length of the whole
interval. Suppose that $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ is a bounded function on the
compact interval $I=[a,b]$ with
$$
M=\sup_I f\quad \& \quad m=\inf_I f.
$$
If $\mathcal{P}$ is a partition of $I$, let 
$$
M_k=\sup_{I_k}f\quad \& \quad m_k=\inf_{I_k}f.
$$
Note that these suprema and infima are well-defined, finite real numbers since
$f$ is bounded. Moreover
$$
m\leq m_k\leq M_k<M.
$$
If $f$ is continuous on the interval $I$, then it is bounded and attains its
maximum and minimum values on each subinterval, but a bounded discontinuous
function need not attain its supremum or infimum.




Further, we define the **mesh** or **net** of the partition by
$$
||\mathcal{P}||=\max_i(x_i-x_{i-1}).
$$
We say that $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$ if there exists a real number
$I$ such that for all sample points $\xi_i\in[x_{i-1}, x_i]$
$$
\lim_{||\mathcal{P}||\to 0}\sum_{i=1}^n f(\xi_i)(x_i - x_{i-1})=I,
$$
that is, as we make the mesh finer and finer this sum (of rectangles)
approaches some constant. That common limit (if it exists) is denoted by
$$
\int_a^b f(x)~dx.
$$

![Reimann Sums (Source: [Wikimedia](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Integral_Riemann_sum.png))](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/2c/Integral_Riemann_sum.png?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original){width=400}


## Riemann Integrability

Riemann integrals are the first type of integrals we are introduced to in our
study of calculus due to their ease of interpretability and their utility for
application to smooth and continuous functions. However, it is not too
challenging to define a function that is not Riemann integrable, for example

:::{.definition data-title="Riemann Integrability"}

A bounded function on a compact interval $[a,b]$ is Riemann integrable if and
only if it is continuous almost everywhere.

:::


## Properties of Riemann Integrals

Throughout, $f$ and $g$ are Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$. The proofs below use
the definition of the integral as a limit of Riemann sums, together with the
criterion above for integrability (continuity almost everywhere).

:::{.theorem data-title="Algebraic Properties"}

For constants $\alpha,\beta$ and $a<c<b$:

1. **Linearity:** $\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and
   $$
   \int_a^b (\alpha f(x)+\beta g(x))~dx = \alpha\int_a^bf(x)~dx + \beta \int_a^b g(x) ~ dx.
   $$
2. **Additivity over intervals:**
   $\displaystyle\int_a^bf=\int_a^cf+\int_c^bf$.
3. **Products and absolute values:** $fg$ and $|f|$ are integrable.

:::

:::{.proof}

(1) A Riemann sum is linear in the function,
$\sum(\alpha f+\beta g)(\xi_i)\Delta x_i=\alpha\sum f(\xi_i)\Delta x_i+\beta\sum g(\xi_i)\Delta x_i$,
and limits are linear.

(2) Take partitions of $[a,b]$ that contain $c$ as a node (refining a partition
by adding a point does not change the limit as the mesh tends to $0$). Such a
Riemann sum splits into a sum over $[a,c]$ and a sum over $[c,b]$, and the limit
of each piece is the corresponding integral.

(3) If $f$ and $g$ are bounded and continuous almost everywhere then so is $fg$,
and $|f|$ is continuous wherever $f$ is, so both are integrable by the
criterion.

:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Order Properties"}

1. **Monotonicity:** if $f\le g$ on $[a,b]$ then $\int_a^bf\le\int_a^bg$.
   In particular $f\ge0$ implies $\int_a^bf\ge0$.
2. **Bounds:** if $m\le f\le M$ then
   $$
   m(b-a)\le\int_a^bf\le M(b-a).
   $$
3. **Triangle inequality:** $\left|\displaystyle\int_a^bf\right|\le\displaystyle\int_a^b|f|$.

:::

:::{.proof}

(1) If $f\le g$ then every Riemann sum of $f$ is at most the corresponding sum
of $g$, since $\Delta x_i>0$, and the inequality is preserved in the limit.

(2) Apply (1) to the constants $m\le f\le M$ and use $\int_a^bc=c(b-a)$, which
is clear since every Riemann sum of a constant equals $c(b-a)$.

(3) We have $-|f|\le f\le|f|$, and $|f|$ is integrable, so by (1) and linearity
$-\int|f|\le\int f\le\int|f|$.

:::

**Orientation convention.** We define $\int_b^af:=-\int_a^bf$ for $a<b$ and
$\int_a^af:=0$. With this, additivity $\int_a^bf=\int_a^cf+\int_c^bf$ holds for
any ordering of $a,b,c$.

:::{.theorem data-title="Mean Value Theorem for Integrals"}

If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ there exists $c\in[a,b]$ with
$$
f(c)=\frac1{b-a}\int_a^bf(x)~dx,
$$
that is, $f$ attains its average value.

:::

:::{.proof}

Let $m,M$ be the minimum and maximum of $f$ on $[a,b]$, which exist since $f$
is continuous on a compact interval. By the bounds above the average
$\frac1{b-a}\int_a^bf$ lies in $[m,M]$, and by the intermediate value theorem
$f$ takes every value in $[m,M]$.

:::

### Which Functions are Integrable?
By the criterion above, the following are Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$:

- every **continuous** function,
- every **monotone** function (it has at most countably many discontinuities),
- every bounded function with **finitely many** (or countably many)
  discontinuities.

Changing the values of an integrable function at finitely many points changes
neither its integrability nor the value of its integral.

### The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
The Riemann integral and the derivative are inverse operations.

:::{.theorem data-title="Fundamental Theorem of Calculus"}

Let $f$ be integrable on $[a,b]$.

1. Define $F(x)=\int_a^xf(t)~dt$. Then $F$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, and if $f$
   is continuous at $x$ then $F$ is differentiable at $x$ with $F'(x)=f(x)$.
2. If $G$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ with $G'=f$, then
   $$
   \int_a^bf(x)~dx=G(b)-G(a).
   $$

:::

:::{.proof}

(1) For $f$ bounded by $K$, $|F(x+h)-F(x)|=\left|\int_x^{x+h}f\right|\le K|h|$,
so $F$ is continuous. If $f$ is continuous at $x$ then
$$
\left|\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}-f(x)\right|
=\left|\frac1h\int_x^{x+h}\big(f(t)-f(x)\big)dt\right|
\le\sup_{|t-x|\le|h|}|f(t)-f(x)|\to0
$$
as $h\to0$.

(2) For any partition $\{x_0<\dots<x_n\}$ the mean value theorem for $G$ gives
points $\xi_i\in(x_{i-1},x_i)$ with
$G(x_i)-G(x_{i-1})=f(\xi_i)(x_i-x_{i-1})$. Summing (the left side telescopes),
$$
G(b)-G(a)=\sum_{i=1}^nf(\xi_i)(x_i-x_{i-1}),
$$
which is a Riemann sum of $f$. Letting $\|\mathcal{P}\|\to0$ the right side
tends to $\int_a^bf$.

:::

Part (2) turns the evaluation of integrals into finding antiderivatives; see
[[calculus-of-simple-functions]] for tables of standard ones, and
[[leibniz-integral-rule]] for differentiating integrals that depend on a
parameter.

## Examples

:::{.example data-title="An Integral from the Definition"}

Compute $\int_0^1x^2~dx$ directly from Riemann sums. Since $f(x)=x^2$ is
continuous it is integrable, so the limit can be computed along any sequence of
partitions with mesh $\to0$. Take the uniform partition $x_i=i/n$, so
$\Delta x_i=1/n$, with right endpoints $\xi_i=i/n$:
$$
S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac in\right)^2\frac1n=\frac1{n^3}\sum_{i=1}^ni^2
=\frac{1}{n^3}\cdot\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}=\frac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{6n^2}.
$$
As $n\to\infty$ (mesh $=1/n\to0$)
$$
S_n=\frac{2n^2+3n+1}{6n^2}\to\frac26=\frac13.
$$
This agrees with the fundamental theorem: $\int_0^1x^2dx=\left[\tfrac{x^3}3\right]_0^1=\tfrac13$.

:::

:::{.example data-title="A Function with a Jump"}

Let $f=1$ on $[0,\tfrac12]$ and $f=2$ on $(\tfrac12,1]$. It is bounded with one
discontinuity, so it is integrable, and by additivity
$$
\int_0^1f=\int_0^{1/2}1~dx+\int_{1/2}^12~dx=\tfrac12+2\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac32.
$$
Note that $f$ has no antiderivative on $[0,1]$ (derivatives satisfy the
intermediate value property and $f$ skips the values between $1$ and $2$), yet
it is integrable. So the integral exists in cases where part (2) of the
fundamental theorem does not apply.

:::

:::{.example data-title="A Function that is Not Riemann Integrable"}

The **Dirichlet function** on $[0,1]$,
$$
f(x)=\begin{cases}1&x\in\mathbb{Q},\\0&x\notin\mathbb{Q},\end{cases}
$$
is bounded but is discontinuous at *every* point, so it is not Riemann
integrable. Directly: every subinterval of any partition contains both rational
and irrational points. Choosing all sample points $\xi_i$ rational gives every
Riemann sum equal to $\sum\Delta x_i=1$, while choosing them all irrational
gives $0$. The sums therefore do not converge to a single number as the mesh
tends to $0$.

The [[lebesgue-integral]] handles this function: it equals $0$ except on the
countable set $\mathbb{Q}$ of measure zero, so its Lebesgue integral is $0$.

:::
